item.title: Why Seatsy went global: from Stamford Bridge to Madison Square Garden
item.dc:creator: Tom Giles
item.description: Tom Giles, cofounder and MD of Seatsy, on why Seatsy grew from premium hospitality into a global marketplace, with the NBA, NFL and US arenas now on the site.
item.content:encoded:
When Lewis Allsopp and I started Seatsy, the plan was always bigger than one city or one sport. We wanted to build a place where people could book the best seats at the events they care about most, wherever those events happen to be. This year we took the biggest step yet towards that, and I want to explain why it matters to the people who book with us.

From hospitality to a genuine marketplace

We went live in March 2026 with a focus on premium hospitality: the lounges, the dining, the days that people plan their year around. That is still at the heart of what we do. But the people we look after do not follow just one league or one country. Their year might include a Premier League weekend, a Grand Prix, a Knicks game and a big arena show, and we wanted Seatsy to cover all of it.

In July we answered that with a new API partnership with a US based provider. It gives Seatsy direct access to inventory for the NBA, the NFL and major US concert venues, including Madison Square Garden. At the time I said:

“This new API partnership is the single biggest step forward we've made from a platform perspective, and there's more to come.”

Tom Giles in the Seatsy newsroom, July 2026

I still feel exactly the same way. It changed what Seatsy is. We are no longer only a premium hospitality partner. We are becoming a proper global marketplace for sport and music.

Why American sport, and why now

More and more people plan travel around sport. A trip to New York is no longer just about the sights; for a lot of people it is about a night at the Garden. A long weekend in the States now often starts with the fixture list, and the hotel gets booked around it.

That is the behaviour we built for. You can now browse NBA tickets on Seatsy, see what is coming up at Madison Square Garden, and book a game such as Utah Jazz at New York Knicks just before Christmas. For NFL fans, there are fixtures like Cleveland Browns at New York Giants at MetLife Stadium in December. The same booking journey works for a Premier League afternoon in London as it does for an NFL Sunday at MetLife Stadium.

Inventory is only half the job

Access to more events is exciting, but it means nothing if the experience of booking is clunky. Alongside the new partnership, we rolled out improvements across seatsy.com to make it easier to choose the right block or package and to get hold of your tickets. That matters to me just as much as the events themselves.

My years working in sport taught me that people remember the whole day, not just the result. If the booking feels uncertain, the build up to the event feels uncertain too. So every order is covered by our ticket guarantee, and if you cannot see the event you want, our team will try to source it for you.

What has not changed

Going global does not mean losing what made us different. We still care most about the experiences that turn a ticket into a memory. Our hospitality experiences are still where a lot of my energy goes, from a table at Bagatelle at Stamford Bridge to a full Dublin weekend for Ireland v England in the Six Nations.

Seatsy is independent. We source tickets and packages through established hospitality providers and resale partners, and we are open about that. Trust is the product, and it is the one thing we will never compromise on as we grow.

What comes next

We are working on further integrations across the GCC, and there will be more to share in due course. The ambition Lewis and I set out on day one has not moved: one trusted place for the best seats in sport and music, wherever in the world they are.

If you are planning a trip around a game or a gig next year, take a look at what is live on Seatsy, or read more about who we are. And if there is an event you want that you cannot find yet, tell us. We want to hear about it.

item.title: Advice for anyone wanting to get into the sports industry
item.dc:creator: Tom Giles
item.description: Tom Giles shares practical advice for breaking into sport, drawn from more than ten years in partnerships, fan engagement and now founding Seatsy.
item.content:encoded:
I get asked one question more than any other: how do you get into the sports industry? It usually comes from someone who loves sport, has watched it all their life, and cannot see the door in. I have spent more than ten years working in sport, from partnerships at Bath Rugby to the activation team in fan engagement at Chelsea FC, and now cofounding Seatsy. Here is the advice I would give anyone starting out.

Loving sport is the starting point, not the pitch

Almost everyone applying for a job in sport loves sport. That is not what sets you apart. What sets you apart is understanding that sport is a business, and showing you can help that business work. Clubs and rights holders need people who can sell, organise, create, analyse and look after partners and fans. Lead with the skill you bring, then let the passion show in how you talk about it.

Learn how partnerships really work

Working on partnership deals at Bath Rugby, with brands such as Thatchers, Dyson, Jaguar Land Rover and Opro, taught me that a partnership is a relationship, not a logo on a board. A brand wants to reach people, and the club wants a partner who stays. The best deals happen when both sides understand what the other is trying to achieve.

If you want to work in commercial roles, start learning that language now. Read about sponsorship, follow how brands show up around big events, and ask yourself why a partner chose that property. That curiosity comes through in an interview far more than a list of favourite teams.

Matchdays teach you everything

At Chelsea, I was part of the activation team in fan engagement, helping corporate partners such as Yokohama Tyres, Hyundai, EA Sports and Hublot bring their activations to life, especially on matchdays. A matchday is the best classroom in sport. Everything has a deadline, the details matter, and the fans notice when something is not right.

My advice is to get as close to live events as you can. Volunteer, work event days, help at a local club. You learn how a day is planned and delivered, and you meet people who do the jobs you want.

You do not need contacts to start, but you do need to build them

Plenty of people worry that they cannot get into sport without knowing someone. Contacts help, but nobody starts with them. You build them. Be useful, be reliable, follow up, and stay in touch with people long after a role or a project ends. The industry is smaller than it looks, and a good reputation travels.

The skills that matter most

  • Communication. Writing a clear email and speaking well to a partner or a fan never goes out of fashion.
  • Commercial thinking. Understand where the money comes from and what the customer actually wants.
  • Organisation. Live events reward people who plan properly and stay calm when plans change.
  • Resilience. It is a competitive industry. Keep going.

Sport is bigger than the clubs

Working for a club is not the only way in. Agencies, brands, media, technology and travel all live around sport, and some of the most interesting opportunities sit there. That is the path I took when Lewis Allsopp and I cofounded Seatsy, a marketplace for premium sports and music hospitality. Everything I learned about partners, fans and matchdays now goes into how we put together hospitality experiences built around the event.

Starting a business also taught me that the same principles hold. Know your customer, care about the details, and make the day memorable. Whether it is a table at Bagatelle at Stamford Bridge or a weekend away for a big fixture, the experience around the event is what people remember.

One last thing

Stay curious about the industry. Read about it every day, watch how events are changing, and form your own view. Our Seatsy newsroom is a good place to start, with guides such as the football derbies worth travelling for this season.

If you are trying to break into sport, keep knocking on doors. The people already inside were once exactly where you are now.

item.title: The seat is only half of it: where premium hospitality is heading
item.dc:creator: Tom Giles
item.description: Seatsy's view on Lord's, Benfica and the A's ballpark, and why fans now book the whole day, not just the seat.
item.content:encoded:
Three stories landed this month that say a great deal about where live sport hospitality is heading.

The first came from Lord's. The Stadium Business reported that MCC has made Gullivers Sports Travel the first official short breaks partner of Lord's, the first time the ground has given a travel company match day tickets to sell with accommodation. The second came from Lisbon, where Benfica and Emirates have opened a new lounge for 160 guests at the Estádio da Luz, with food led by Vítor Matos, whose restaurants have earned six Michelin stars, according to Coliseum. The third came from Las Vegas, where the most exclusive club at the A's future ballpark has sold out 17 months before the stadium opens.

Different sports, different continents, same message. People are not just buying a seat any more. They are buying a day. That is the view we take at Seatsy.

The trip is becoming the product

The Lord's news is a useful sign of how venues now think about the whole visit, not only the ticket. An official short breaks partner packages travel and a stay with a day at the ground, which is already how many people want to plan a big fixture. A Test match or a final is rarely a two hour appointment. It is a reason to leave home, to stay the night, and to make a weekend of it.

The Ashes are back in England next summer, and a day like the opening day of the Ashes Test at The Oval is the sort of occasion that rewards planning the whole trip around it, not just the seat. At Seatsy, we see the same pattern across sport. The seat matters, but the memory is usually made of everything around it: how you arrive, where you stay, who you are with, and how the day is looked after.

The great grounds have always sold a sense of occasion that starts long before the first ball and carries on long after the last. What is changing is that more of the industry is building products that match that truth.

Food has become the front row

Benfica bringing in a chef of Vítor Matos's standing tells you clubs now see the dining room as part of the product, not a side room. A lounge is no longer an afterthought. It is part of why someone chooses one experience over another.

The same shift is visible across the calendar. On Seatsy, Bagatelle at Stamford Bridge is one of the hospitality options available around a match. The standard we look for is simple. Great food, great service and a great view of the event, brought together so the day can unfold in one place.

When dining is treated as part of the event, people stay longer and remember more. That is as true in Lisbon as it is in London, Las Vegas or anywhere else the best days in sport are sold.

Selling out before the stadium exists

The A's story is worth underlining for anyone who still thinks premium is a niche. A club behind home plate, built around dining and hospitality, gone well over a year before the first pitch is thrown. Demand for the very best experiences is running ahead of supply, and it is happening everywhere.

That has a practical meaning for anyone planning a big date. The most sought after tables, boxes and suites do not wait for the fixture list to feel close. They go early, sometimes before a stadium has even opened its doors. It is one reason Seatsy puts experiences built around the event alongside the tickets themselves. Whether it is a hosted weekend at the Ryder Cup at Adare Manor or a table for a big night at a ground, the idea is the same. The event is the reason you go, and everything around it is what you remember.

What is worth planning for 2027

  • Book the experience early. The best tables, boxes and suites go first, often long before the fixtures feel close.
  • Think in trips, not tickets. Travel, a hotel, a dinner the night before. That is what turns a match into a memory.
  • Ask for what you cannot see. If the thing you want is not listed, ask. Good hospitality teams can often find it.

Live sport has always been about the people you share it with. What is changing is that the industry is building more of the day around that truth. We will keep writing about the dates worth planning for here and on the Seatsy newsroom. If you want to see what is coming up next, Seatsy is the place to start.

item.title: Building Seatsy: Tom Giles in his own words
item.dc:creator: Tom Giles
item.description: Tom Giles, cofounder and Managing Director of Seatsy, on why he and Lewis Allsopp built a premium ticketing marketplace in Dubai, told in his own words.
item.content:encoded:
In March 2026, Tom Giles and Lewis Allsopp opened Seatsy, a premium sport and music ticketing marketplace built in Dubai. Since then the business has been covered by Arabian Business, Smashi Business, Dubai Eye 103.8's Business Breakfast and EVENTFAQS Middle East. This is the story so far in Tom's own words, from The Seatsy Story podcast with Lewis, Seatsy's announcements and his own posts, with a link to every source.

Why Seatsy

Tom spent more than a decade inside professional sport, at Chelsea FC, MCC at Lord's and Bath Rugby, before going out on his own. At Chelsea he was in the activation team in fan engagement, helping corporate partners such as Yokohama Tyres, Hyundai, EA Sports and Hublot with commercial activations on matchdays.

“I worked for rights holders, biggest rights holders in sport, Chelsea, Lords Cricket Ground, Bath Rugby, like the biggest brands in their respective sports, but I wanted something for my own.”

Tom on The Seatsy Story with Lewis Allsopp, from 20:00

When the two founders launched, they put the ambition in one line.

“Two founders, two complementary skillsets, and one shared obsession: building the global standard for premium hospitality ticketing. We are going big, and we are going fast.”

Tom and Lewis Allsopp in the Seatsy launch announcement

Born in Dubai

The idea grew out of a gap Tom and Lewis saw in the Gulf. Tom described it on LinkedIn a few weeks before launch as “Seatsy is a new Sport & Music premium ticket marketplace, born in Dubai but will serve a global market.”

“If somebody from Dubai or Abu Dhabi or Qatar or Saudi wanted to go to the Premier League, they're probably going to the UK sites. … This is born and bred in the UAE.”

Tom on The Seatsy Story with Lewis Allsopp, from 12:00

Lewis made the market case to Arabian Business: “People in the UAE spend more on hospitality, sports and music per head than anywhere else in the world”.

Trust first

Premium tickets are a market with a trust problem, and Tom has been blunt about it.

“there's so many touts out there. There's so many agencies that are giving sports hospitality industry a bad name. Whereas this is going to be a trusted site where you know what you're buying.”

Tom on The Seatsy Story with Lewis Allsopp, from 11:00

“this is straight from the source. It's going to be a seamless experience. And through my experience in the sports industry, I know that we're buying with trusted … sources.”

Tom on The Seatsy Story with Lewis Allsopp, from 27:30

The product was designed around how people actually buy.

“So, first things first, this is built for mobile. You're going to be browsing on your mobile. The most important feature for us, like any tech business, is the search bar.”

Tom on The Seatsy Story with Lewis Allsopp, from 35:00

Official Ticket Seller in Dubai

In September 2026, Dubai's Department of Economy and Tourism approved Seatsy as an Official Ticket Seller.

“This is a huge moment for Seatsy. Dubai is one of the fastest growing live events markets in the world, and being an approved DET Ticket Seller means we can now bring our platform and our promise of a premium, seamless fan experience to every event in the city.”

Tom in the Seatsy DET announcement

“We have spent months building the compliance, the technology and the relationships to get here, and we are ready to move fast.”

Tom in the Seatsy DET announcement

Bath and Dubai

A month earlier, Seatsy opened a UK base in Bath, Tom's home city, alongside its Dubai headquarters at Meydan Grandstand.

“We're building Seatsy for the long term. This isn't simply about taking another office. It's about investing ahead of where we want the business to be”

Tom in the Seatsy Bath headquarters announcement

“This investment will allow us to build a sales team in the UK focused on getting our customers to the biggest events in the world.”

Tom in the Seatsy Bath headquarters announcement

The new office came with a welcome surprise: “Best part: the previous company had a HUGE Bath Rugby (The Rec) wallpaper on the wall! Was meant to be.”

The clients

Summer 2026 showed who Seatsy is for. On the first day of Wimbledon, Tom wrote about clients on Centre Court, fans in Boston for the World Cup and corporate guests at Trent Bridge: “All of which are customers from UAE, travelling overseas for major sporting events in UK & USA.”

“Perks of the job? Absolutely, but also the kind of networking that actually matters.”

Tom on LinkedIn, June 2026

What comes next

“we're becoming a genuine marketplace, with access to the biggest events in the world, from the NBA and NFL to the world's top artists.”

Tom in the Seatsy US partnership announcement

“We're building a serious sales function, and this is a chance to get in early and grow with us as we set our sights on some of the biggest events in world sport.”

Tom in the Seatsy commercial team announcement

For Tom, the product is only half of it.

“Now it's just adopting like the right mindset and bringing the right people on the journey. That's the key thing for me.”

Tom on The Seatsy Story with Lewis Allsopp, from 20:30

Every quote above links to its source. Podcast quotes come from automatic captions of The Seatsy Story, so timestamps are approximate.

item.title: In his own words: nine marathons in nine days for Jenson
item.dc:creator: Tom Giles
item.description: Tom Giles on running from Bath to Land's End for his son Jenson and CureSHANK, told in his own words from podcasts, interviews and his own posts.
item.content:encoded:
In the summer of 2025, Tom Giles ran from Bath to Land's End: nine marathons in nine consecutive days, from 27 June to 5 July, for CureSHANK, the charity funding research into Phelan McDermid Syndrome. His son Jenson lives with the condition.

Tom, the cofounder and Managing Director of Seatsy, based between Dubai and the UK, has talked about the run on podcasts, in the press and on his own channels. This is the story in his words, with a link to every source.

Why take it on

When he announced the challenge in February 2025, Tom was honest about his starting point.

“I have only run one marathon prior to this, so this will test me in every possible way”

Tom on LinkedIn, February 2025

On the Ambitious Minds podcast with Jay Lawrence, he explained why he chose something so big.

“recently took on a challenge where I ran nine marathons in nine days. I did that because I wanted to capture attention and once you've got attention people will listen.”

Tom on the Ambitious Minds podcast, from 41:45

Who he was running for

Jenson collapsed when he was two days old and spent the first weeks of his life on life support at Bristol Children's Hospital.

“there was a point in time where I didn't think that he would survive. So, he was on life support for weeks in Bristol.”

Tom on the Ambitious Minds podcast, from 41:00

He was later diagnosed with Phelan McDermid Syndrome and Ring 22, a combination so rare that only a few hundred people in the world share it. Speaking to the BBC, Tom described the boy behind the diagnosis as “funny, handsome and obsessed with cars, tractors and bikes”, adding: “He has a smile that would light up a room”.

“Jenson is the most loving and handsome boy. He lights up every room.”

Tom speaking to GB News

Bath to Land's End

The route ran through Glastonbury, Chard, Exeter, Okehampton, Liskeard, Charlestown, Falmouth and Penzance before the finish at Land's End. Most days came in well over marathon distance, something Tom was quick to point out when his cofounder Lewis Allsopp brought the run up on The Seatsy Story: “You're doing me a disservice there as well. It was pretty much ultramarathons.”

“This was the hardest thing I’ve ever done. The adrenaline on the first few days was insane, but it wasn’t until day four that I truly struggled.”

Tom speaking to GB News

Family joined him along the way. His daughter ran the closing miles of some stages with him, and Jenson was there with him at the finish line at Land's End.

“She finished a few of the runs with me, and we’ve got videos of our two-year-old crossing the finish line with me. It was very emotional.”

Tom speaking to GB News

Writing on LinkedIn afterwards, he summed up the distance as “392 kilometres and 509,640 steps away from the start line in Bath on 27th June.”

What it started

The run raised more than £24,000 for CureSHANK and sparked Race for Research, a global campaign with runners across five continents. As Tom told Somerset Live: “What started as 'Run for Jenson' turned into 'Race for Research'”.

“Every step I take is for Jenson and the thousands of people worldwide living with PMS who deserve breakthrough treatments and a brighter future”

Tom, quoted by CureSHANK

Looking back, he described the nine days as “emotional, rewarding, and purposeful.” And he was clear about what they were really for.

“This was never just about running. It was about giving my son a voice, giving families like ours hope, and doing something meaningful in the face of something incredibly difficult. I couldn’t be prouder of Jenson, of our family, and of the people who supported us.”

Tom speaking to GB News

Read and listen

  • Ambitious Minds podcast with Jay Lawrence
  • BBC News: Dad's hope to find cure for son's rare condition
  • GB News: Best of Britain
  • Somerset Live
  • The News International: Hero dad runs 9 ultra-marathons in a row for son’s rare genetic disease
  • The Sun: My boy, 4, can’t walk or talk yet but desperately tries – his condition is so rare it baffles doctors
  • CureSHANK: Race for Research

Tom now spends his working life building Seatsy, the premium sports and music hospitality marketplace, and putting together experiences for 2027. The lessons from those nine days come with him.

item.title: Day four: what nine marathons taught Tom Giles about resilience
item.dc:creator: Tom Giles
item.description: The hardest moment of Tom Giles's run from Bath to Land's End, and the mindset he and his family rely on, in his own words.
item.content:encoded:
Every endurance story has a low point. For Tom Giles, cofounder of Seatsy, it came on day four of nine, somewhere between Exeter and Okehampton, on his 2025 run from Bath to Land's End for his son Jenson and the charity CureSHANK.

The low point

Tom had run just one marathon before he committed to nine in a row. He told GB News the first few days carried him.

“This was the hardest thing I’ve ever done. The adrenaline on the first few days was insane, but it wasn’t until day four that I truly struggled.”

Tom speaking to GB News

Then came the morning of day four.

“I woke up alone, my ankle swollen from a tweak the day before, and realised I wasn’t even halfway yet. That was a really tough mental moment – I honestly questioned whether I could keep going.”

Tom speaking to GB News

He kept going. Five days later he reached Land's End, and more than two weeks after that he wrote on LinkedIn:

“It's been over 2 weeks since I completed 9 marathons in 9 consecutive days, I'm still riding the high and it's only just starting to sink in!”

Tom on LinkedIn, July 2025

His headline for that post was simple: “Anything is possible when you are fuelled by purpose”.

A glass half full family

Tom is clear that the mindset was not built for the run. It comes from home, and from life with Jenson, who has Phelan McDermid Syndrome. On The Seatsy Story with his cofounder Lewis Allsopp, he put it like this:

“my wife and I like it's all about trying to stay optimistic.”

Tom on The Seatsy Story with Lewis Allsopp, from 16:45

“Kim and I have always been like you know us like we're glass half full type of people, blue sky people.”

Tom on The Seatsy Story with Lewis Allsopp, from 17:45

He said much the same to Somerset Live.

“We don't feel sorry for ourselves, we don't feel sorry for him.”

Tom speaking to Somerset Live

And on the Ambitious Minds podcast he gave the credit to his wife, Kim, who, as he puts it, has almost become Jenson's full time carer: “I couldn't do it without her.”

Training for the rest of life

The habits that got him to Land's End now shape the rest of his week. Speaking to Jay Lawrence, Tom said:

“without exercise, I wouldn't function.”

Tom on the Ambitious Minds podcast, from 47:00

“you're trying to get like that 1% better every day and like you're trying to be a better husband, a better dad, a better colleague, a better business, but like I love the challenge”

Tom on the Ambitious Minds podcast, from 47:45

He even applies the language of training to family life: “I am training to be more present at home.”

What comes next

He is now training for a full Ironman, and the running has not finished either.

“I’d love to do something again in 2027. In the meantime, my wife and I might do a few smaller challenges – a couple of marathons to raise awareness, probably without asking for money. This isn’t the end.”

Tom speaking to GB News

The same patience shapes how he builds Seatsy between Dubai and the UK: steady progress, the right people around you, and a lot of turning up. See what the team is working on in the Seatsy newsroom or explore 2027 experiences.

Source clips: Ambitious Minds, The Seatsy Story, GB News and Somerset Live.

item.title: Why Tom Giles went public about Jenson's rare diagnosis
item.dc:creator: Tom Giles
item.description: Tom Giles on sharing his son Jenson's Phelan McDermid Syndrome diagnosis, the search for answers and why awareness mattered as much as fundraising.
item.content:encoded:
When Tom Giles ran nine marathons in nine days in 2025, the money was only part of the point. The cofounder of Seatsy set out to raise funds for CureSHANK, to raise awareness of Phelan McDermid Syndrome, and to educate people about rare conditions. That meant sharing his family's story in public.

The search for answers

His son Jenson was diagnosed after months of uncertainty, through a genetic test. Tom told Somerset Live:

“the journey to diagnosis is the hardest part.”

Tom speaking to Somerset Live

“If he never had those tests, we probably still wouldn't know.”

Tom speaking to Somerset Live

He knows the family were fortunate in one respect. As he told the BBC:

“We were lucky to get a diagnosis as quickly as we did because some parents don't get one for a long time.”

Tom speaking to BBC News

Why he shared it

Tom had used his own channels for sport and business for years. In 2025 he turned them over to Jenson's story. On the Ambitious Minds podcast he explained why:

“I was authentic. I tried to be authentic. I tried to show vulnerability. I talked about everything that we've gone through”

Tom on the Ambitious Minds podcast, from 43:15

“if I found somebody like me when we got that diagnosis who was talking that openly and had a really nice family lifestyle … and was trying to bring about positive change. I would have felt a lot better when I was scrolling in the hospital”

Tom on the Ambitious Minds podcast, from 43:30

He made the same point on LinkedIn after the finish:

“I would have loved to stumble across this when we first received the news, so hopefully one person has benefited from this.”

Tom on LinkedIn, July 2025

Awareness as much as money

The fundraising went far beyond the original goal, but Tom told GB News that was only half of it.

“We massively exceeded our fundraising target, which was incredible. But the awareness was just as important.”

Tom speaking to GB News

“I wanted to educate our friends, our community, and social media followers about these incredibly rare disorders. Most people haven’t heard of Phelan McDermid Syndrome or Ring 22, but they need to.”

Tom speaking to GB News

He also wants more families to ask about genetic testing.

“Researchers think that a lot of people who are diagnosed with autism could potentially have PMS. Some people don't get diagnosed until they're 20.”

Tom speaking to Somerset Live

Hope for research

CureSHANK funds work towards treatments for people with Phelan McDermid Syndrome, and Tom's hopes are practical.

“I hope our story helps accelerate research. There are real scientists working right now on life-changing treatments, and donations make a tangible difference.”

Tom speaking to GB News

“I hope they find a cure or life-changing therapy that significantly improves Jenson's quality of life.”

Tom speaking to BBC News

“hopefully by raising a lot more awareness and one day trying to find a cure, somebody getting that same diagnosis will be a little bit more informed”

Tom on the Ambitious Minds podcast, from 44:45

To learn more or support the research, visit CureSHANK. Tom is based between Dubai and the UK, where he leads Seatsy; you can see the experiences the team has built for 2027.

Source clips: Ambitious Minds, BBC News, GB News, Somerset Live, The News International, The Sun and Tom on LinkedIn.

item.title: Six months live: what building Seatsy has taught me so far
item.dc:creator: Tom Giles
item.description: Tom Giles, cofounder and MD of Seatsy, on going live in March 2026 and becoming a DET Official Ticket Seller in Dubai.
item.content:encoded:
On 24 March 2026, Seatsy went live. Lewis Allsopp and I built it as equal partners, with one simple idea at the centre of it: the best seats in sport and music should be easy to book, and the whole experience around them should feel looked after.

I am proudest of the team that made the first six months happen, in Dubai and in our UK office.

Trust is the product

Ticketing lives or dies on trust. When someone books a weekend around a fixture, they are not really buying a ticket. They are buying the certainty that the day will go the way they imagined it.

That is why being approved as an Official Ticket Seller by Dubai's Department of Economy and Tourism mattered so much to us. It is not a badge for the website. It is a promise to every customer that we do this properly.

Build around the moment, not the seat

Thirteen years in sport, at Lord's with MCC, at Chelsea and at Bath Rugby, taught me that people remember the whole day: the arrival, the hospitality, the company, the journey home. So we build around the moment.

You can see it in the Seatsy experiences we have put together for 2027, from a full Dublin weekend for Ireland v England to a Ryder Cup stay at Adare Manor, a short walk from the first tee.

What being a founder actually feels like

The calendar never stops. Some weeks I am in Dubai, some weeks I am in the UK, and most weeks there is a big event somewhere that needs looking after. I would not swap it.

I am a dad of three, and my family keeps everything in perspective. My son Jenson has Phelan McDermid Syndrome, and running nine marathons in nine days for CureSHANK in 2025 taught me more about pace, patience and people than any business book. Now I am training for a full Ironman. Building a company feels very similar. You do not win it in a day. You keep turning up.

What comes next

More of the events people genuinely care about, done properly. If you want to see what is live, start with football, Formula 1 or concerts, or read more about who we are.

Thank you to everyone who has booked with us, backed us and pushed us in these first six months. We are only getting started.

item.title: The 2027 dates I would put in the diary first
item.dc:creator: Tom Giles
item.description: Tom Giles picks the 2027 sport and music dates worth booking now, from Ireland v England in Dublin to Oasis in Glasgow and the Ryder Cup at Adare Manor.
item.content:encoded:
Every year I get asked the same question: what should I book now, before it goes? For 2027, my answer is already clear. The big ones are on sale, and the people who plan early get the year they actually want.

Here are the dates I would put in the diary first. The full list, with ten picks, is in my Founder's Hot Picks on the Seatsy newsroom.

Ireland v England, Dublin, 5 February

The opening night of the 2027 Six Nations, at the Aviva Stadium. Rugby has been a huge part of my life, and this is the trip I would not miss. There are Ireland v England tickets, and a full Dublin weekend hosted by former Ireland full back Geordan Murphy.

Oasis at Celtic Park, 21 May

Some nights you simply have to be in the room. Oasis in Glasgow is one of them. Oasis tickets are on Seatsy now, and my advice is to sort the stay at the same time as the ticket.

El Clasico, Madrid, 9 May

Real Madrid v Barcelona at the Santiago Bernabeu in the spring. The biggest club game in world football. El Clasico is live on the site.

The Monaco Grand Prix from Cap Ferrat, 3 to 7 June

A calm base in Saint Jean Cap Ferrat, with a short tender into Monaco. This is how I would do the race. The Monaco stay is open for enquiry.

The Ryder Cup at Adare Manor, 16 to 20 September

If there is one week of 2027 I would tell you not to leave late, it is this one. The Ryder Cup stay at Adare Manor runs from 12 to 20 September, a short walk from the first tee.

Book the right one, not all of them

Football dates can still move for television, so always check before you book travel. And if you want a second opinion on a weekend, get in touch. I would much rather you book the right event than every event. You can browse everything live on Seatsy whenever you are ready.
